report:
## Conclusion

Yes — there is reasonably good, though still limited, evidence that olive leaf extract (rich in the polyphenol oleuropein) can modestly lower blood pressure, particularly in people with mild/borderline hypertension.

The strongest evidence comes from a double-blind, randomized, active-controlled trial (Susalit et al., 2011) in stage-1 hypertensive patients, which found that 500 mg twice daily olive leaf extract reduced systolic and diastolic blood pressure comparably to the standard drug captopril over 8 weeks ([nutraingredients.com](https://www.nutraingredients.com/Article/2011/03/09/Olive-leaf-extract-may-help-hypertension-Frutarom-study/); [scholar.ui.ac.id](https://scholar.ui.ac.id/en/publications/olive-olea-europaea-leaf-extract-effective-in-patients-with-stage/)). A separate double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 60 prehypertensive/mildly hypertensive subjects also reported significant reductions in both systolic and diastolic pressure after 8 weeks of supplementation versus placebo ([adamoshien.com](https://www.adamoshien.com/post/uncovering-the-benefits-of-oleuropein-in-blood-pressure-reduction)).

More recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses—including one focused on cardiometabolic effects in adults with prehypertension/hypertension, and a 2022 meta-analysis of herbal supplements (Antioxidants journal)—generally support a beneficial, blood-pressure-lowering effect of olive leaf extract, alongside favorable effects on lipids and inflammation, though effect sizes are modest and study numbers are still relatively small ([aor.ca](https://aor.ca/research-library/olive-leaf-extract-effect-on-cardiometabolic-profile-among-adults-with-prehypertension-and-hypertension-a-systematic-review-and-meta-analysis/); [v2-examine-dev.vercel.app](https://v2-examine-dev.vercel.app/conditions/high-blood-pressure/)).

**Bottom line:** Olive leaf extract shows promise as an adjunct for mild hypertension, with effects roughly comparable to low-dose antihypertensive medication in one trial. However, evidence is based on relatively few, small-to-moderate trials, and it should not replace prescribed blood pressure medication without medical supervision.
